1.2 Purpose of the well

The well had several objectives:

- Prove commercial volumes of hydrocarbons.

- Test the Urd stratigraphic trap and a minor structural closure.

- Test channel and "low amplitude" seismic facies.

- Test the Hermod reservoir in a position that could be tied back on seismic to the provenance area in the west.

- Prove hydrocarbon migration route.

1.3 Result of the well

The well was spudded in a water depth of 109 m and drilled to a total depth of 2475 mMD RKB. Both the predicted reservoirs, the Hermod Formation and Ty Formation were encountered (figure 4.2). Both reservoirs are of good quality, but without hydrocarbons. This was verified by logs, a water sample and laboratory studies of the cores. There were no indications of hydrocarbons from cuttings, sidewall cores or wireline logs in other parts of the well either.

Except for the top Utsira Formation, the observed formation tops are in accordance with the prognosis and well within the expected error bars (see table 4.2 and figure 4.1 and 4.2).

4 Geological Report

4.1 Geological setting

Licence 245, blocks 25/3 and 25/6, is located east of the Frigg and Heimdal Fields, on the east flank of the Viking Graben. The distance to the Norwegian coast is 145 km. Well 25/6-3 is the third well drilled within block 25/6-3, but the first well in PL 245. (Block 25/6 was first licenced as PL 117 in 1985 with Saga as operator. Most of the area was relinquished in 1992. Norsk Hydro took over Saga 01.01.00.). In the area there are several oil and gas discoveries, both in Jurassic and Tertiary formations.

The drilled prospect is named Urd and the reservoir, the Hermod Formation, consists of channel/fan deposits of Early Eocene/Late Paleocene age. Urd is a combined structural/stratigraphic trap, with pinch outs to the northeast, east and south and with a spill point at 2175 m RKB to the west-northwest.

4.3.2 Geological Summary

NORDLAND GROUP                                      134.0 - 925.0 m RKB
                                                    (109.0 - 900.0 m MSL)

Series: Miocene to Holocene.
Depositional environment: Glacial marine, inner to mid shelf.

The complete Nordland Group was drilled with returns to seafloor. The section from 195 to 925 m RKB
is interpreted from the MWD logs to consist mainly of various clays/claystones with interbedded sands,
including the sanddominated Utsira Formation.

Utsira Formation                                   652.0 - 925.0 m RKB
                                                    (627.0 - 900.0 m MSL)

Series: Miocene to Oligocene.
Depositional environment: Inner to mid shelf.

The Utsira Formation consists of sand/sandstones with interbedded claystone layers.
No samples of the lithology were available due to returns to seafloor.

HORDALAND GROUP                                    925.0 - 2020.0 m RKB
                                                    (900.0 - 1995.0 m MSL)

Series: Upper Oligocene- Lower Eocene (top not seen)
Stage:
Depositional environment: Outer shelf to lower bathyal

The Hordaland Group consists of claystones with stringers of limestone and dolomite. Traces of loose
sand occur.

The claystones are olive grey to olive black, firm, occasionally moderately hard, blocky, silty to slightly
silty in parts, slightly micromicaceous and micropytic. They are furthermore glauconitic and non
calcareous in the upper part. The claystones become medium dark grey to dark grey, olive grey and dark
green grey towards the lower parts.

In the lowermost part, the claystones become varicoloured and occasionally tuffaceous.

The limestone stringers seen throughout the formation, consist of moderately hard, off white, light brown
or pale yellow brown, micritic to crystalline and occasionally argillaceous limestones.

The dolomite stringers are yellow brown to dusky brown, hard to very hard, angular to blocky,
microcrystalline to cryptocrystalline, and occasionally sucrosic.

Traces of clear, fine to coarse, angular to rounded, loose sand/quartz grains were observed throughout the

# 6 Drilling Report

## 6.1 Rig move, positioning and anchor handling

### 6.1.1 Summary

Both the rig move and the anchor handling were conducted in fair weather.

The rig was towed 124 Nm from block 9/2 (Yme) to the location of 25/6-3 by Maersk Master in 33.5 hours with an average sailing speed of 3.7 Nm/hr.

The rig positioning and deployment of the anchors was performed efficiently and in full accordance with the plan. All twelve anchors were run, the rig ballasted to drilling draft and the anchors pre-tensioned to 150 tons without problems in 18.5 hours.

### 6.1.2 Experiences / Recommendations

- The anchors were pull tested to maximum tension just after they were run. Because of the limited amount of time the anchors are allowed to settle this increases the risk of dragging. Pull test the anchors to working tension after they are run, and wait to pull test anchors until after the 20" casing is run.

- The main contributing factor to the success of the operation was the use of the "Racal" positioning system. All three boats had this system onboard and were thus fully utilised during the operation. Future positioning/anchoring operations will benefit considerably if a similar operation is planned.

- Prior to the rig move, Dolphin informed Statoil that the maximum permitted tensional loading on the towing bridle was 70 tons which was equal to 80 % of the documented limit. It was later disclosed by Dolphin that Statoil had been misinformed and the actual maximum permitted tensional loading was approx. 120 tons (80 % of the 150 tons limit). If the correct information had been provided at the outset, the sailing speed could have been increased, resulting in less time consumption for the rig move.

held back to ensure a vertical hole. A significant reduction in ROP was experienced through the
final 15 m of the section where the average ROP was approx. 3 m/hr. Harder drilling through the
latter part of the hole section indicated the possible presence of minor boulders. Despite a lower
ROP, this proved not to be problematic and there was no significant inclination deflection of the
well.

Unnecessary time was spent reaming the lower interval of the 36" hole section due to inclination
measurement errors in the Anderdriift tool (Ref. 6.2.2).

Upon completion of the drilling phase, the well was displaced to 1.35 SG mud. The 30"
conductor and permanent guide base was run and cemented in place. There was a minor problem
with the supply of cement mix water during the cement job, but this did not affect the quality of
the job.

The PGB bulls eyes showed 0.5°.

**Bottom Hole Assembly**

- If boulders are expected, it is recommended to run a stiff BHA to ensure a vertical hole is

6.4.2 Experiences / Recommendations

### Drilling Bit

- In these formations, the Hughes MX09DX button rock bits gave good performance. Bit ROP was 23.6 m/hr and overall ROP was 15.5 m/hr before coring. After coring, bit ROP was 14.4 m/hr and overall ROP was 10.8 m/hr.

### Drilling Fluid

- Anchor/M-I Drilling Fluids Sildril™ mud system proved to give excellent inhibition, keeping the instable clay formations in lower Hordaland and upper Rogaland Gruops in check. With other types of water based mud systems, these formations have been known to swelling and sloughing after being exposed for 5-7 days. Not so in this case; the well bore was in excellent condition the 11 days the 8 1/2" hole was open. However, due to the skin that this mud builds on the formation it is necessary to wipe the drilled hole every 5 stands drilled. Once the hole is wiped once, however, it remained in excellent condition.

In addition, only minor problems were experienced with bit balling. The first 8 1/2" BHA balled up from behind the bit and up to the near bit stabiliser. There was no bit balling tendencies after this one incident.

- Recommendation: This drilling fluid system is recommended in future applications where instable clay formations are encountered and at the same time, where pseudo oil based or oil based muds can not be used.

- Recommendation: Ensure that the mud properties are at their optimum before starting on a new section.

- The Sildril mud was premixed onshore and sent out to rig. Due to rough weather, there was logistical problems getting all the required mud chemicals onboard the rig in time. This caused the Sildril mud system not having optimum properties when starting the section (and when balling up).

### BHA

- A very short near bit stabiliser (70 cm total lenght) was included in the first 8 1/2" BHA to get MWD/LWD sensors as close to the bit as possible. However, this BHA balled up from behind the bit and up to the near bit stabiliser. No such tendencies were reported on the next BHA's, included the last where a "normal" near bit stabiliser was used (192 cm total lenght).

- Recommendation : Use a standard near bit stabiliser if it is suspected that the flow will be hindered by the stabiliser.

## Cementing 30" Conductor

### Cement Mixing & Pumping Rates

#### Overview of Event

The desired cement mixing and pumping rates were not achieved during cementing operation on
the 30" conductor. This is due to the ineffective operation of the water supply line control valve.
Restricted water flow into the mixer limits the ability to mix and subsequently pump the cement
at the desired rates.

#### Conclusion(s) & Recommended Action(s)

Halliburton to repair or if required replace the valve/control unit. Preventative maintenance
procedures should be checked and verified.

## General Discussion

When writing detailed procedures one should try to be as specific as possible whenever possible.
For example, if a max. parameter value is specified, i.e.: ROP, pump rate etc. it should be
adhered to. By stating such things as "or as hole conditions dictate" ambiguity is introduced into
the statement. This will not apply in all cases but whenever possible such things should be
avoided.

## Comments from Dolphin & Service Companies

### Work Capacity of the Drill Crew during Rig Rove and Spud Activities

#### Overview of Event

During the rig move and subsequent spudding operations it was noticed that the Dolphin drill
crew were overstretched with activities relating to anchoring and pre-spud preparations on the
drill floor, deck and moonpool areas. The capacity of the standard crew was strained and
prioritising of activities was necessary to ensure the required work was performed at the desired
time.

# ANDERGAUGE INVESTIGATION REPORT ADF117

Customer : Statoil				Date of run : 21 October 1999
D.D. Company : N/A				AG Engineer : Alan Howie
Well Name : 25 / 6-3 URD			Date of Report : 3 November 1999
Rig : Byford Dolphin				Prepared by : Alastair Macfarlane
Job No. : NAD318					Tool Serial No. : AD931/ ASF873b

---

## Summary

Anderdrift tool ADB931 (Flask no. ASF873b) was to be utilised to monitor inclination in the
36" conductor hole section of Byford Dolphin 25 / 6-3 URD. The tool was tested 25m above
sea bed at 2270 lpm and was observed to be returning approximately 20 Bar pulse height (11
pulses were returned initially (factory set survey) followed by a 5 degrees +). The high angle
test survey was accepted since the unconstrained BHA was likely to drift in sea currents
(water depth was 137m).

When on bottom the Anderdrift returned a 1/2 degree (10 pulse) survey at 4350 lpm. The survey
pulse height was only 2 to 3 Bar and was initially difficult to read however confidence was high
since characteristic pressure drop off of approximately 10 Bar was observed after each survey.

Drilling continued with surveys of 0 and 1/2 degrees returned until the final 10m. At this stage
the inclination jumped inexplicably to between 2 1/2 and 3 degrees. Again trouble-shooting
procedures were applied however the measured inclination remained high and the Anderdrift
finally stopped pulsing (after a pill was pumped at 1000 lpm). A single shot dropped at TD
showed hole inclination at less that 1/2 degree.

## Inspection and function testing

On 26 October Andergauge flew a Service Engineer from Aberdeen to Stavanger in order to
conduct a visual inspection on the Anderdrift flask ASF873b. The tool had not been due to
arrive at Andergauge's service facility for several days and with other similarly set up tools
due for imminent dispatch a preliminary investigation was considered essential.

When the Anderdrift tool was broken out of the hole opener assembly and the flask removed
the external surfaces of the flask were observed to be packed with mud/gel. This was
removed by hand. Two significant observations were made;

- A number of pieces of rubber and fibre were found on top of the integral Anderdrift
screen.

- A slender piece of steel (approximately 57mm long x 7mm square - see photograph

The steel debris was removed in order to check tool function. The flask was then held as close to vertical as possible and the pulse head forced down with a steel bar and hydraulic jack (this simulates mud pump flow). When the pulse head was released the tool returned smoothly to the 1 degree position. This basic test indicated that the tool was functioning after removal of the steel debris.

Upon return to Aberdeen ASF873b was immediately placed in the Andergaue flow loop for flow testing. Flow rates between 1250 lpm and 2420 lpm were used with fresh water. Three different downstream orifice sizes were tested (0.601 in2, 0.785 in2 and 2.761 in2). The tool functioned to specification during approximately 20 survey cycles. Note that the jig used to test the tool could only be set up close to vertical therefore the majority of surveys returned only 10 pulses equating to ½ degree inclination. Sample results are contained at the rear of this report.

The rigorous post job calibration test was successfully passed and strip down inspection showed all components to be in good condition.

## Conclusion and Discussion

The cause of failure on Byford Dolphin 25 / 6-3 URD can be attributed to metal debris jamming the pulse head/pulsing system. ASF873b had returned correct surveys of ½° and 0° until 189m (11m above TD) where the inclination inexplicably jumped to approximately 3° (5 pulses). Subsequent repeated surveys proved unreliable varying between ½° (10 pulses) and 2½° (6 pulses) before the tool finally stopped pulsing.

The unreliable surveys obtained prior to the Anderdrift shutting down are typical of what might be expected when debris is located loosely above the pulse head but inside the pulsing system. As the tool attempts to record a survey (when the pumps are stopped) the debris is carried upward with the pulse head until movement is arrested by random interference between the pulse head and a pulse ring. The Anderdrift finally stopped returning surveys when the debris became jammed between the pulse head and pulsing system close to the drilling position.

## Recommendations

Andergauge recommend that surface drill pipe screens be utilised whenever there is likelihood that long slender debris may contaminate the mud system.

It should be noted that all Anderdrift flasks are fitted with an integral screen as protection against debris. The screen effectively prevents most types of harmful debris from entering the tools' pulsing system. The only exception to this is long slender debris that can, under exceptional circumstances (orientation), bypass the screen.
